I experience profound joy upon learning that the *Tantravārttika*, composed by Kumārila Bhaṭṭa— a work of auspicious benediction— is being published together with the *Ajitā* commentary written by Paritoṣamiśra. [This is] the commentary of Paritoṣamiśra.

Until now, it has not been published anywhere. Therefore, this is an unprecedented opportunity for scholars, and especially for students of Mīmāṃsā, to understand the *Tantravārttika*. It has been prepared by the learned professor Dr.
Kiśoranātha, along with his collaborators Dr. Kamalanayan Śarmā and Kumārī Arcanā Caturvedī.

Since this work has been edited by Śubhodayā with great effort, preceded by a careful examination of the readings against five manuscript sources, the editor fully deserves praise. Furthermore, the Principal of the Gaṅgānātha Jhā Kendrīya Saṃskṛta Vidyāpīṭha also merits our thanks for the publication of this book.

Having read the pages of the bound manuscript, it was understood that the reading preserved in the *Ajitā* commentary would be capable of resolving doubts regarding the uncertain passages of the *Tantravārttika*. Not only this,
but in many places, it would facilitate the comprehension of the meaning of the root text.

Among the three commentaries on Śabara’s Bhāṣya composed by Kumārila— namely the *Ślokavārttika*, the *Tantravārttika*, and the *Ṭupṭīkā*— philosophers show a great inclination toward the *Ślokavārttika* alone, as it provides an examination of various philosophical systems (*darśana*). Nevertheless, the *Tantravārttika* also contains extensive discussions on the technicalities of the scriptures (*śāstra*).

Following the authority of reasoning (*yuktipramāṇa*), the *Tantravārttika*, which is endowed with invincible [arguments], is therefore to be saluted in every way. He hopes that by means of this work, the tradition of Mīmāṃsā, which has reached a state of decline, may become strong once more. Guwahati.

In the catalogues (*mātṛkā*), this work is indicated by the title *Tantraṭīkānibandhana*, meaning "A Treatise on the Commentary on the Tantra. However, at the end of the third chapter, the author himself, by writing a single verse, supports the name *Ajitā* for it:
"Since this *Ṭokā* was composed by one dwelling on the banks of the Ajitā, with his sins washed away by its waters,
may it therefore be known by the name 'Ajita'.
Although there is no river anywhere well-known by the name Ajitā, [the author refers here] to Ajita, that is, Nārāyaṇa.

I believe that this very river—which is found on its bank in the form of the Śālagrāma, which is renowned as the Śālagrāmī in Nepal, and which is known elsewhere by the name Gaṇḍakī—was intended by Ajita, the preeminent among Mīmāṃsakas, under the name Nārāyaṇī; Indeed, in the *Mīmāṃsā-kusumāñjali*, the great scholar Mahāmahopādhyāya Umeś Miśra establishes that this [author] was a Maithila born in the thirteenth century of the Sṛṣṭi era; therefore, his residence likely lay on the banks of the Nārāyaṇī river.
At that time, Mīmāṃsā was firmly rooted in Mithilā through the practices of study, teaching, and the composition of texts.
It has been propagated and flourished, and thus it does not require further effort to establish its existence.

When a specific purpose is obtainable, why should we assume an unexpressed result? If it is argued that the context (*prakaraṇa*) is sublated by the syntactical connection (*vākya*), we say no, because there is no contradiction. He also accepts the incitement found in the passage beginning with "The udumbara is indeed strength" (*ūrg udumbaraḥ*). It must be said: due to proximity (*sannidhi*), that [reason] is understood as being delimited by that very [subject]. However, if the invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*) between the status of being a means of preparing food—which resides in items such as a ladle or a cooking pot—and the connection with the *homa* offering were not inferred, then nothing either heard or seen in the text would be rendered intelligible. Even in the world, upon seeing smoke from grass, it is inferred that there is specifically a fire of grass, not merely fire in general. Just as the application of the word "cow" (*go*) is established as referring to the specific cause [of the dewlap] and not merely to any animal that moves, so too, because the winnowing basket (*śūrpa*) is designated as the cause for the preparation of food, there is no contingency of its causal function applying to other things. In this case, the meaning would be as follows:
whatever winnowing basket is capable of preparing food, by that alone one should offer the oblation; there is no inclusion of the ladle, the pot, and so forth. Just as...

When fire is strongly blown upon, it is stated that it is the cause of burning; yet that very fire, when not blown upon, does not burn, whereas conch shells and the like, even when strongly blown upon, do not burn. Therefore, there is a fixed distinction (*vyavasthā*). Furthermore, if one intends to express a "great generality" (*mahāsāmānya*) other than the specific function of preparing food performed by the winnowing basket (*śūrpa*), then whatever is apprehended would possess some degree of being a cause for food.

Because the term "exists" is not fixed [in its application], the word "annakaraṇa" (means of making food), being a mere restatement of whatever substance is implied by the oblation, would be purposeless. Therefore, it is better that it serves as a praise on account of being a cause for food—namely, "whatever is a means of making food, such as the winnowing basket. In this way, the specific nature of being a winnowing basket (*śūrpattva*) is understood through the subordinate commonality of being a means of making food (*annakaraṇatva*).

This indicates that [the term] "that which has the capacity for making food" (*annakaraṇasamartha*) is a secondary characteristic (*upalakṣaṇa*) of the winnowing basket (*śūrpa*). Thus, even in the case of the statement "the winnowing basket is capable of making food," it is not the case that the capacity for making food is a qualifying attribute (*viśeṣaṇa*) of the winnowing basket, because the winnowing basket is the subject being restated (*anuvāda*).
And if the winnowing basket were the qualificand (*viśeṣya*), then that alone would be the result of the reason; therefore, it is not sufficient as a reason—thus concludes the summary.

What, then, is the distinction between injunction, restriction, and exclusion? It is said: an injunction applies when [an action] is not established at all; a restriction applies when [it] is optionally established.

For an injunction (*vidhi*) is indeed differentiated in this way by some specific feature. In that case, where it is understood that something was absolutely unestablished (*atyantāprāpta*) and will not have been established prior to the statement [of the injunction], there the application (*niyoga*) is a pure injunction (*vidhi*), as in "he sprinkles the rice-grains" (*vrīhīn prokṣati*).

In the first chapter, the *saṃhitā* was composed without depending on grammar at all; likewise, in the *Mīmāṃsā* as well, in the rule "gavyasya ca tadādiṣu" (*Mīmāṃsā-sūtra* 8.1.18), there is that which is suitable for correct usage regarding products and parts of a cow.

The word *śabda* is employed elsewhere specifically in reference to the Gavām Ayana sacrifice. Similarly, in the rule "If it be argued that it is so for the two heavens" (Mīmāṃsā Sūtra 6.3.18), although one ought to have said "of heaven and earth" (*dyāvāpṛthivyoḥ*), the term is used many times in a manner devoid of its defining characteristic. Likewise, a Gṛhya author, when he ought to have said "smelling at the head" (*mūrdhanyabhighrāṇam*), employs the substitute form *jighra* in the incorrect form "smelling upon the head" (*mūrdhanyabhijighrāṇam*).

Even when grammar is complete, there are many usages characterized as deficient in the *Nirukta*, just as in the case of the etymological derivation of the word "brāhmaṇa" from "bruvaṇāt" (from speaking) in the passage,

"saṃvatsaraṃ śāṃśayānāḥ," where, while providing the etymology of the word "brāhmaṇa" regarding frogs found in that mantra, [the author] shows that its basis is the quality of being prone to speaking, according to the rule *bruvo vaciḥ* [Pāṇini 2.4.53].
It was used [in this way] because it was spoken without even performing the grammatical substitution of *vacya*.
There is no end to ungrammatical forms (*apaśabda*) in the *Itihāsas* and *Purāṇas*, nor is there an end to those who practice elephant training and the like, using forms such as *ubhābhyādi*.

The expression *ubhābhyām*— meaning "by both [tusks]" as in "the blow delivered by both tusks simultaneously"— is employed by all, including Pālakāpya, Rājaputra, and others, entirely independent of grammatical rules. Furthermore, such usages are extremely numerous in the Vedas and are accepted by the students of those texts.

First, regarding the sūtra [Pāṇini 1.4.30]: *janikartuḥ prakṛtiḥ*.
For here, by the rule "the suffixes *iṣ* and *tip* indicate the verbal root," the word *jani* is understood to be the verbal root itself, as it conforms to that definition.

It is explained as follows: In the rule *janikartuḥ prakṛtiḥ*, it is intended that the *prakṛti* (source) of "that agent" (*tasya kartuḥ*) is designated by the technical term *apādāna*. However, the word *jani* is not at all covered by this definition in its capacity to denote the meaning of "that which is being born" (*jāyamānasyārthasya*).

Therefore, like the word "horse" when used for a poor man, this [word *jani*] is understood to be grammatically incorrect (*asādhuh*) with respect to that meaning, because it denotes merely the act of being born (*janimātra*). Likewise...

By employing a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*) which is prohibited by the rule *tṛjakābhyāṃ kartari* (Pāṇini 2.2.15), there is an abandonment of the fruit of grammar. Likewise, the compound in the rule *tatprayojakaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.4.55) is likewise prohibited. Similarly, even in the Vārttika it is stated: "It is established because the mention of the radical *haL* in the root *dambh* refers to the genus (*jāti*)."

Likewise, regarding the rule "But there is a change of state because of the intervention of time-words" (*ānyabhāvyaṃ tu kālaśabdavyavāyāt*), here, having laboriously constructed a compound, and then, by virtue of that compound designation, the designation "quality-word" (*guṇavacana*) being sublated, the suffix *ṣyañ* was applied by the rule "from quality-words, *brāhmaṇa*, etc. (*guṇavacanabrāhmaṇādibhyaḥ*) even though it was not actually connected [to the base]. In the *Bhāṣya* as well, it is said "by the maxim of the goat and the sheep" (*aviravikanyāyena*).

[276] Examples such as *śam* and others have been cited; yet they do not differ from worldly [usage] merely because of the citation of specific sentences, since sentences are not formally explained by grammar. Therefore, certain [forms] are indeed Vedic, such as *gṛbhṇāmi* and *datvāyātha*.

Examples such as these are appropriate to be cited, not examples such as "aśaṃ no devī. Furthermore, why would an example from the Vedic language (chāndasa) be obstructed by the immediately preceding rule, "when [the word] is established" (siddhe) and "from common usage" (lokataḥ)? Moreover, if the grammatical description were to apply to worldly (laukika) words, then words such as *gāvī* and the like would be even more appropriately described, since their usage is well-established.

Their worldly nature arises from their non-usage in the Vedas. As for words such as *go* (cow) and others, however, it can be said that they were extracted again and again from the Vedas by those who study them. Thus it was also stated by Manu:
"In the beginning, he fashioned the various social orders separately from the very words of the Veda" (*Manusmṛti* 1.21).

Even today, Vedic scholars (*śrotriya*) are seen to cite entire mantras—even those whose meaning is identical to common worldly speech—when they wish to express a mundane sense; how much more so, then, for individual quarters (*pāda*) or words? Furthermore, there is no need for a grammatical rule (*lakṣaṇa*) for Vedic words whose recitation has been handed down word-for-word; nor is there any grammar superior to that which comes from the mouth of a teacher.
By stating "because the Vedic meter follows what is observed," it is shown that the definition itself is of little utility, as it is dependent upon traditional recitation (āmnāya).
Just as the definition of agriculture and such is useless because it is already established by worldly convention,
so too is the definition of words established by the Veda useless.

they are not [valid] purposes either, because such things are established elsewhere or because they are only slightly established even from this [grammar].

Third Pāda:
Endowed with the *Ajitā*,
the Veda is thus preserved in its entirety by fellow students themselves.
Even if one has perished through the corruption of one's own syllables, others will not tolerate it out of hatred.
Therefore, because the compassionate teachers and others are devoted [to the Veda], it is impossible for anyone to destroy the Veda; thus, it is preserved by them.
Therefore, grammar must first be studied for the sake of preserving the Vedas; however,
in the world, meanings are established through common usage even without grammar,
both in everyday transactions and undoubtedly in poetry and the like.

[281] However, if grammar were to be resorted to for the sake of its utility in Sanskrit poetry— even though it is not employed in the sentences of everyday discourse— according to the principle of the definitions of poetry and drama, Prakrit grammar, and the *dvipadī*, *rāsaka*, and so forth;

Nevertheless, it is argued that because there is no restrictive rule for the composition of poetry and no scripture governing its origin, it would be possible to compose literary works in whatever languages one pleases; thus, there would be no fixed standard regarding words.
However, even with respect to the beauty of poetry, this [lack of restriction] is not at all useful.
For it is due to the fault of grammarians that they employ difficult Vedic meters.
Nor should one employ a non-worldly definition, thinking "there is no definition";
for if usage is already established in the world, a definition would be purposeless.
Therefore, even in the world, the protection of words is never achieved through grammar.
And thus:
"Grammar is not purposeful even for the sake of the modification (ūha) of words."
Since modification (*ūha*) is also established from another source, it is like the option regarding what is to be modified and what is not to be modified.

Mantras employed in the archetype (prakṛti) by virtue of their primary visible purpose, their own inherent meaning, or their combined meaning, proceed to the ectype (vikṛti) through the extension of the ritual function (kāryātideśa).

But if [it is argued that] these [terms] belong to conventional (samvyavahāra) speech, then this is the explanation for [the claim that] there is no doubt even in cases such as poetry (*kāvya*) and the like. "Having its own meaning" means having a primary, perceived purpose. In this way, modification (*ūha*) occurs if the mantras have their primary meanings in the archetype (*prakṛti*).

They are employed for the purpose of manifesting the meaning; they have their own purpose as primary, provided that their meanings are inherent and they are prompted by the *apūrva*. Likewise, if they proceed in the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*) by following the assistance transferred [from the archetype], and if in the modified sacrifice something else—such as a substance or a deity—takes over the function of the archetypal element, then there is a visible purpose (*dṛṣṭārthatā*) therein.

It is established in the section on Mantras (Mantrādhikaraṇa) that [the mantra] is for the purpose of manifesting a visible object; for if that were not the case, the unseen result (*adṛṣṭa*) would be accomplished by the mere utterance of the unmodified [mantra], and thus there would be no modification.
In that regard, the fact that the purpose is the manifestation of a visible object is established by the conclusion of the Mantrādhikaraṇa. (Āpadevīya Mīmāṃsānyāyaprakāśa, Section 36).

In the Jyotiṣṭoma, Darśapūrṇamāsa, and other sacrifices, ritual duties (*dharmas*) are prescribed. Are these prompted by the root *yaj* (sacrifice), or rather by the *apūrva*?

When there is doubt as to whether [the rites] are prompted by the *yajati* (sacrificial act), it is initially concluded that they are prompted by the *yajati*, because the root *yaji* is not enjoined as the primary element, and because one hears of them in connection with both the sacrifice and its means in such injunctions as "one should sacrifice with rice" (*vrīhibhir yajeta*) and "one threshes the rice" (*vrīhīnavahanti*). To this, it is replied:

The sacrificial act is the primary element, for it is the object of the Vedic injunction; the purification (*saṃskāra*) applied to the substances is prompted by that [act], because it exists for the sake of that [act].

then if it were accepted as such, its status as an auxiliary to the Veda (vedāṅgatva) would be contradicted.

From the rules "from *kali*, [the suffix] *ḍhak*" [Pāṇini 4.2.8] and "from *vāmadeva*, [the suffixes] *ḍyaṅ* and *ḍyau*" [Pāṇini 4.2.9], the grammarian acquires the understanding that these denote Sāmans seen by the seers Kali and Vāmadeva. However, in the Veda, it says:
"From that, desirable wealth (*vasu vāma*) came into being; therefore it is the *Vāmadevya*"; and "Because he measured out (*akālayat*), that is the *Kāleya*."

The observation of word-derivations in passages such as "yat tvam" contradicts the understanding that follows grammatical rules. Likewise, because the authors of the Kalpasūtras— such as in the cases of "kṛṣṇaśaṃvāsaḥ" and "kṛṣṇavalakṣe ajine"— rely on explanations like "having black fringes" and so forth, there are meanings of Vedic sentences that remain uncomprehended even by a hundred grammars, yet are obtained through the tradition of those who know the meaning of the Vedas.

And the meanings of words such as *yūpa* (sacrificial post), understood through their preceding and following context, are also explained. For example, in cases such as these, according to grammar, the word *sthūlapṛṣatī* is said to mean "a female ox" (*anaḍvāhī*) due to its similarity [to the word for ox]; or else, when there is doubt as to whether it means "that which has large spots" (*sthūlāni pṛṣanti yasyāḥ sā sthūlapṛṣatī*), the fact that it is established by the students [of the Veda] as having the acute accent on the first syllable serves as an indicator [that it is a *bahuvrīhi* compound] in grammar.
Because it is explained by that [grammar] through the determination of the *bahuvrīhi* compound, there is a determination of its meaning. Regarding the term *kuśalodāra*:

based on conformity with grammar (*vyākaraṇa*), the word *kuśala* is understood to mean "one who cuts *kuśa* grass" (*kuśasya lātari*), and the word *udāra* to mean "one who rises up" (*udgantari*). However, from usage (*prayoga*), the word *kuśala* also applies to one who is skilled (*pravīṇa*) in other activities; yet, it refers specifically to the excellence of intention (*āśayotkarṣa*).

Just as those endowed with the Ajita [sūtra] attain an understanding of the meaning without doubt, so too should it be explained regarding the meanings of words such as *sthūlapṛpatī*.
Only tradition (paramparā) is capable of providing a definitive determination; thus, grammar need not be relied upon. Furthermore:
"Regarding the meanings of sentences, thousands of doubts arise;
yet from grammar, not even a single prima facie argument (pūrvapakṣa) concerning these can be understood."

If grammar were intended for the purpose of resolving doubts regarding the meaning of the Vedas, then one must consider: do the *arthavādas* (explanatory passages) convey some independent meaning, or are they subordinate to something else? Likewise, is the "obtainment of vigor" (*ūrjavarodhana*) the actual fruit of using *audumbara* wood, or is it mentioned merely for the sake of praise? Similarly, [one must distinguish between] injunctions based on reasons (*hetuvidhi*), explanatory passages stating reasons (*hetvarthavāda*), and the application of mantras, as well as those whose purposes are seen (*dṛṣṭārtha*) or unseen (*adṛṣṭārtha*).

[Grammar] would remove doubts regarding the singular number of the cup (*graha*) in passages such as "he takes the cup" (*tvādigraha*), and so forth. Now, if it is argued that such matters are not introduced in grammar because they are already established by Mīmāṃsā, then it is all the more unnecessary to rely [on grammar] for the purpose of determining the meaning of a few coarse details, such as the "speckled cow" (*sthūlapṛṣatī*), which are established by the statements of the authors of the Kalpasūtras. Furthermore—
Even when doubt arises regarding the derivation of a word's meaning from its etymological characteristics, the resolution comes solely through interpretation;
for even in the case of Vedic words, interpretation cannot be prevented by force.
By this very technical rule (*paribhāṣā*), "the specific meaning is understood through explanation" (*vyākhyānato viśeṣapratipattiḥ*),
one cannot say "it is not the Veda because of doubt," just as one cannot say "it is not a grammatical rule because of doubt."
Furthermore, the Veda cannot be explained by anyone who has not grasped the meaning of words through recourse to grammar; for it is from that [grammar] that certainty may arise.
Just as the Veda exists, so too does its interpretation exist at all times;
therefore, an interpretation of [terms such as] *sthūlapṛṣatī* and the like is not possible without grammar.
Furthermore, the accentuation of words as they are used in common worldly discourse is not observed;
therefore, there can be no determination of meaning based on an accent that falls outside of conventional usage.

The determination of word-meanings depends upon the linguistic usage of the elders (*vṛddha-vyavahāra*). In that context, because there is no distinction in usage—such as between a compound having an acute accent on the final syllable (*samāsāntodāttatva*) or the original accent of the prior member (*pūrvapada-prakṛtisvaratva*)—there can be no fixed determination of specific meanings based on those [accents]. For instance, the word *dāra* does not apply to rising smoke and so forth. Regarding "the original accent of the prior member": it is unaccented (*anudātta*).

Regarding the rule *padamekavarjam* (Pāṇini 6.1.158): in a compound, when there is a single word (*aikapadya*), one syllable per word is udātta; however, in that case, one [of these] is set aside, and the other remains as its original accent (*prakṛti*). In this regard, the rule *bahuvrīhau prakṛtyā pūrvapadam* (Pāṇini 6.2.1) applies; because the first member of the compound retains its original accent (*prakṛtisvara*).

"Regarding the fact that a *bahuvrīhi* compound has its initial syllable accented: now, although there is no etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*) of word-meanings in the Veda, [it remains] doubtful...

both always [in general] and specifically in the *brahmayajña*, the constituent elements of sacrifice (*dravyayajña*), and the silent recitations (*japa*).

there is no determination of meaning by means of the accent prescribed in grammar.

Therefore, grammar should not be studied even for the sake of removing doubt; for this is not a science that produces the application of specific accents which constitute a factor for determining the meaning. Some [arguments] appear to have a semblance of purpose, while others are devoid of any means of valid cognition (*apramāṇaka*).

Furthermore, there is a definitive conclusion (*nirṇaya*) reached through the context of the subject matter and other factors; and therein, of a word endowed with a specific accent (*svaraviśeṣa*),...

From its perception, we shall understand that this object possesses precisely that nature; for otherwise, one might suspect how the essential form common to two objects could reside in only one of them. Anticipating this objection, he says: "In that case too, whatever determination may arise... [referring to the fact that] based on observing worldly usage, the form of the word belongs to both meanings.

When it is determined that a word is used with a single meaning, and the apprehension of that single meaning is established through context, subject matter, and other factors, one need not admit that even a word whose accent is unknown to common usage possesses the capacity to convey a specific meaning merely by being included within the totality of conditions for conveying meaning.
Nor [is it necessary] "by what is stated in grammar"; for even by grammar, a word should not be explained as a subordinate factor for the expression of meaning.

The accent (svara) is indeed established, but as a qualifier of the specific form of the correct word (*sādhuśabda*). Such a word is "correct" (*sādhu*). The reason for this is that "this is indeed the instruction on words" (*śabdānuśāsana*). That which is prescribed and for whatever purpose it was commenced is authoritative only therein and not beyond; thus, some [words] are simply fit for usage. If a thing has not achieved its purpose through its primary objectives, then any hope for it in secondary matters is like clutching at kusha and kāśa grass.

In this regard, the prohibition against corrupt words occurs in the context of the explanatory narrative (*arthavāda*) concerning the ancient history of the Asuras, beginning with the passage: "Those who were the Asuras... and so forth.

That which was presented as the purpose has been explained previously exactly as it stands. Furthermore, in the phrase "a defective word" (*duṣṭaḥ śabdaḥ*), the proponent reveals his partiality for his own position by inserting the word *śabda* while extracting a mantra-passage recited by the authors of the *Śikṣā*, which is well-known among many people. Indeed, when a defective mantra is employed, a transgression (*pratyavāya*) for the sacrificer is certainly accepted; as it is said: "Whatever the *Hotṛ* omits..."

For, from such passages as "Speech indeed abandons that sacrificer," we see that when there is a failure of the mantras to be employed by all the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), the fault accrues to the sacrificer. Likewise, the very fault arising from the failure in the application of the mantra "O Indra-śatru, prosper! has been cited as an example. As for what is stated in the *Nirukta*: "That which is studied but not understood is merely recited as a verbal formula (*nigada*)."
"O King, those which are established do not employ grammar; they are merely semblances of purpose.

However, those which do not possess the very forms as they have been presented are without authority. In that regard, as for the statement "those Asuras," when one ought to have said "O enemies, O enemies" (*he araya he araya*), they instead said "te asurā helayo helaya."

Saying this, they were defeated; therefore, a Brahmin must not speak barbarously (*mlecchitavai*). For he who uses an incorrect word (*apaśabda*) is indeed a barbarian (*mleccha*). Thus, because they used the incorrect words "helayo helaya" when they ought to have said [the correct ones], the Asuras were defeated.
A word that is faulty in its accent or its phoneme,
when used incorrectly, is false.
It does not state that meaning.
That vajra of speech destroys the sacrificer.
Just as Indra’s enemy [Vrtra] [perished] due to an error in his accent.

In the mantra "indraśatrur vardhasva" (O you whose enemy is Indra, prosper), if the word *indraśatru* is recited with the acute accent (*udātta*) on its first syllable, it would express the prosperity of the sacrificer, who is the possessor of Indra as his enemy (*indraḥ śatruḥ yasya*), according to the sense of a *bahuvrīhi* compound. However, if it is recited with the acute accent on its final syllable, then, due to that defect of accent, by expressing the prosperity of Indra— the enemy of the sacrificer— according to the sense of a *karmadhāraya* compound, [it would bring ruin] upon the sacrificer.
"It destroys":
that which is studied without being understood is merely recited as a verbal drone.
Like dry fuel in a fireless place, it never burns at all.

In this regard, [grammar] has no utility, because it is not a scripture concerning the performance of ritual acts (*karma*) or their origination. If it is argued that "this is a science of words (*śabda-śāstra*)," then even in those [sciences], there would be no established authority due to the lack of a foundation (*nirmūlatva*), as previously stated. Therefore, it is appropriate that the purpose belongs to the *Kalpasūtras*, *Nirukta*, and *Mīmāṃsā* alone, as they are capable of providing the understanding of the meaning of the studied Mantras and Brāhmaṇas; but this is not the case for grammar (*vyākaraṇa*).

Thus, even when there is a corruption of Vedic words occurring during the study of one's own recitation (*svādhyāya*), teaching, sacrificing, or officiating at sacrifices, if the sacrifice is impaired by that which is based on the *Ṛgveda*—
"Let him not [speak]," it is said; from this statement, it is understood that there is also a restatement of a fault already known.

Furthermore, because we observe the common usage of many people, the term "one who knows the application of speech" (vāgyogavid) refers to a person who has mastered the relationship between words and their meanings, who has determined the specific modes of expression in Brāhmaṇa passages by analyzing the subordinate and primary qualities of things being referred to or enjoined, and who is likewise proficient in the mantras.

Furthermore, it is only one who knows the distinction between the fitness and unfitness for manifesting one's own meaning or the meaning of another—as understood from the injunctions—who is called a "knower of the application of speech" (*vāgyogavid*), not a mere grammarian (*vaiyākaraṇa*); for a grammarian lacks a treatise for the production of such usage. As for the statement of censure, "those who are ignorant," regarding the failure to lengthen the final vowel of a name during a greeting (*pratyabhivāda*), that refers to the *pluta* [vowel], which consists of three morae (*trimātra*).

Since the application of words ending in [specific] suffixes has been established through the instructions of Manu and others based on their worldly renown, this [Vedic passage] lacks the status of an originative injunction (*utpatti-śāstra*) for that usage. Nor does it follow from this cited verse of Manu and others that there is a person who applies [words] by disregarding the distinctions between base and suffix.
Words [are used] correctly at the time of conventional usage for the sake of another.

The knowledge of the distinction between correct words (*śabda*) and corrupt words (*apaśabda*), or its utility, is accepted by way of classification. As for the statement, "The *prayāja* offerings must be performed with their case-endings," that is established through the instruction of the ritual manuals (*yajñika-upadeśa*), and the case-endings of the six-day period are found in the Brāhmaṇa:
"May Agni strike down the Vṛtras," "Agni, the greatest slayer of Vṛtra," and "By Agni, Agni..."

Because we observe the use of both distinct and non-distinct case endings in such passages as "samidhyate," the performance of the *prayāja* offerings—which possess case endings—is accomplished even without grammar, merely by observing the application of those case endings themselves; therefore, grammar is not a necessary science [for this purpose]. Furthermore, it is said: "He who lays down this speech word by word, accent by accent, and syllable by syllable, he becomes fit for the office of the officiating priest (*ātvijīna*)."

Thus it is said that one who has correctly studied the Veda is so designated. Likewise, regarding the verse, "Speech is measured in four quarters," those [explanations] which have been elaborated by the etymologists (nairukta) in accordance with the pursuit of the purposes of the abundance of the fourfold group beginning with the *oṃkāra* and the *mahāvyāhṛtis*—
according to the principle "one should explain [words] even based on the similarity of phonemes and letters"— in those cases grammar (*vyākaraṇa*) has no jurisdiction whatsoever.

As for the reliance on the grammarians' doctrine consisting of the fourfold division of nouns, verbs, prefixes, and particles—that too does not depend significantly on grammar, precisely because this fourfold division is established by common worldly usage. Furthermore, if this were the subject under discussion, the statement, "Humans speak only the fourth part of speech," would be utterly incoherent; for [it would imply that] all four classes of words...

Because it is so stated by human beings, therefore this meaning of the mantra is described as consistent with its preceding and following context: "Speech is measured in four quarters. Those by which speech is expressed or understood—namely, the four means of valid cognition (pramāṇas) known as perception (pratyakṣa), inference (anumāna), comparison (upamāna), and presumptive testimony (arthāpatti)—are thus designated. Among these, those [mantras] that relate to the ritual application of specific words (*pratīka*) and the archetypal...

The [Veda] is understood through three means of knowledge—namely inference, comparison, and presumptive testimony—which arise from observed similarity with modified speech and from what is otherwise unaccountable;

because those [means] establish it, they do not themselves move or utter it. However, that portion which cannot be conveyed by them, the fourth part, which is accessible through direct perception, human students speak and recite.

This is the meaning. Furthermore, from among the six means of valid cognition (*ṣaṭpramāṇī*), two means of cognition have been extracted because they consist of words. First, non-existence (*abhāva*)...
[is as follows].

As for the statement that "the *prayāja* offerings possess case-endings," since case-endings are impossible within the essential nature of the ritual action (*karmasvarūpa*) itself, their possession of case-endings must be understood by way of the deity (*devatā*). Furthermore, because the genitive case is excluded there as well, it is said that there are six [case-endings].
"Speech is measured in four [parts]..."
Those wise Brahmins who possess true insight know those steps.

The syllable *oṃ*, the three great utterances (*mahāvyāhṛti*)—*bhūḥ*, *bhuvaḥ*, and *svaḥ*, and speech itself constitute the fourfold speech.

Alternatively, it refers to the fourfold speech of beasts, birds, reptiles, and humans. Or else, it refers to the fourfold speech according to the distinction between nouns, verbs, prefixes, and particles. The purpose of this abundance of fourfold forms is as follows:

Having extended this principle of word-derivation (*pada-nirvacana*) to the object itself by way of a mere similarity in number, there is not much [to be said].

"Like a means of valid cognition" (*pramāṇavat*); or "because it is included within the category of perception" (*pratyakṣapakṣanikṣepāt*). And thus, it becomes nothing other than perception.

The statement regarding the exclusion of suffixes beginning with *kṛt* containing two, four, or more consonants, as well as the exclusion of *taddhita* suffixes, is accompanied by the term *ajita*.

Since even in grammar (*vyākaraṇa*), the designations of *taddhita* and *kṛt* suffixes are adopted only as they were previously established, and since the measurement of phonemes (*varṇaparimāṇa*) depends on recollection preceded by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), and since qualities such as "possessing resonance" (*ghoṣavattva*) and so forth are enumerated in the *Śikṣās* and *Prātiśākhyas*, and since all Vedic scholars (*śrotriya*) apply these names without difficulty, [there is no contradiction].

Grammar (*vyākaraṇa*) is indeed to be relied upon as a science for the production and application [of words]. Although in the verse "O Varuṇa, you are a good god," the seven case-endings (*vibhakti*) themselves are explained as the "seven rivers," nevertheless, it is grammar alone that either bestows the technical designation (*saṃjñā*) of "case-ending" upon them or adopts what is already well-known. As for those [words] used in actual practice—

Those forms are indeed directly perceived in both the world and the Veda according to their respective divisions; thus, they are not stated in this way merely out of dependence on grammar. However, when the "seven rivers" are understood as actual rivers, or—within the context of praising the sacrificial priests and the patron—as the seven voices belonging to the *hotṛ* priests, or the seven [notes] belonging to the melodies of the *sāman*, or those belonging to its constituent parts, then it is [an] historical [usage].

Since they fall within the domain of ritualists (*yājñika*), they are not the object of grammar at all. Furthermore, once the correctness of Sanskrit words has been established, it must be explained: for what is there a refinement (*saṃskāra*), and how, moreover, is it performed?

When words are being refined through grammar, it is not known what entity is being refined, or what kind of refinement— whether arising (*utpatti*), attainment (*prāpti*), modification (*vikāra*), or the production of something unprecedented (*apūrva*)— is brought about by the power of the means [of grammatical operation] upon those [words] that are distinct [from one another].
First of all, there is no refinement of the universal of "word-ness" (*śabdatva*), the universal of "letter-ness" (*varṇatva*), or of the individual [phoneme] (*vyakti*).
For, due to over-extension in all cases, no systematic determination can be established.

If it were the nature of sound (*śabdatva*) that constitutes correctness, then even mere noises would possess grammatical correctness; and if it were the nature of phonemes (*varṇatva*), then single phonemes as well as corrupt forms like *gāvī* and others would be equally correct.
By this, the refinement (*saṃskāra*) of the manifestation of phonemes (*varṇa*) is refuted.
For if the *ga*-sound and so forth in words such as "cow" (*go*), having been refined once in a particular instance,
were the very same [sound] in words such as "gāvī," it would follow that the latter is likewise correct (*sādhu*).

The forms ending in case-terminations (*vibhakti*) are those such as *deśo'tra* ("the place is here"). Sentences are those whose purpose is the social interaction of friends, or which consist of words expressing friendship. Regarding the term "beginning with voiced consonants" (*ghoṣavadādi*): it refers to the inclusion of a name that begins with a voiced consonant from among the third letters of the classes (*varga*), and likewise has the semivowels (*antasthā*)—*ya*, *ra*, *la*, and *va*—within its middle.

The statement regarding the fruit [of knowledge] belongs to a different context; therefore, because it lacks an invariable connection with the ritual (*kratu*), it is a mere explanatory praise (*arthavāda*), like the scriptural declarations of fruits found in the passages concerning *añjana*, the *khadira* wood, and the absence of dripping.
Furthermore, the injunction of knowledge does not preclude its connection with ritual action.

The obligatory and occasional rites (*nitya-naimittika-karmāṇi*) prescribed for each specific stage of life (*āśrama*) and social class (*varṇa*) must also be performed for the purpose of exhausting previously committed demerit (*durita*) and for the purpose of avoiding future transgressions caused by non-performance. That is to say, since words such as *udbhid* are not established as being invariably preceded by another referent (*arthāntara-pūrvakatva*) at the time of their first cognition—that is, at the initial moment of knowledge—they would, due to their primary occurrence in Vedic usage, function as names (*nāmadheya*) through grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*). Alternatively, it will be meaningful by enjoining a previously unknown action (*apūrva-karma*). Or rather, when there is doubt as to whose name it might be, it is stated [as follows].
The meaning is that upon its production, something unprecedented (*apūrva*) is accomplished for the sake of the sacrifice. What is the reason?
For a quality being enjoined would have to relate either to the fruit or to the ritual action;
yet it is not tenable in any way [to enjoin it] through the cognition of a qualified injunction (*viśiṣṭavidhi*).

First, regarding the injunction of a fruit, there are the following defects: the injunction of a connection with another word, the assumption of a remote relationship, the subordination of the verbal root to another purpose, the sublation of the original *soma* offering, and a sacrifice performed with an implement such as a spade—which is inedible and entirely unprecedented. Likewise, if it were an injunction of a quality (*guṇavidhi*) regarding the sacrifice, the word for the fruit would be rendered meaningless; [and] the *jyotiṣṭoma*, which is already established by its own meaningful desire [for results], [would be sublated].

If [the soma] were a qualifier, there would be a split in the sentence (*vākya-bheda*). Furthermore, the remoteness from the operation of the suffix (*pratyaya-vyāpāra-viprakṛṣṭatā*), the subordination of the verbal root (*dhātu-pārārthya*), and the options regarding the prohibition of eating [the soma] and the prohibition of the sacrifice (*anadanīya-yāga-soma-bādha-vikalpa*) would be utterly untenable. Likewise, in the case of a qualified injunction (*viśiṣṭa-vidhi*), there would be the subordination of everything else (*sarva-pārārthya*), the postulation of multiple injunctive powers (*aneka-vidhi-śakti-kalpanā*), the figurative indication of possessive meaning (*matvartha-lakṣaṇā*), the abandonment of the understood grammatical coreferentiality (*gamyamāna-sāmānādhikaraṇya-tyāga*), and the sacrifice of something unfit for consumption (*anadanīya-yāga*).

These are the defects. Therefore, it is not an injunction of a quality (*guṇavidhi*). He demonstrates this: otherwise, the Vedic revelation (*śruti*) would have mentioned the *udbhid* and other terms as qualities of the ritual (*karma*), because it is impossible to establish a connection [of those names] with the action. Furthermore, their status as producers [of results] is also [dependent on] the quality of the Jyotiṣṭoma.

Thus, because the seed of the relationship—the expectancy—is severed for that which is enjoined after the origin, there is no connection; however, when [the action] is extracted...
When it is taken up by the word, then the expectancy indeed proceeds from the word; and consequently, there is the possibility of a connection with another quality. || 1 ||

Nor can it be understood that this [denotes] either the mere universal (*sāmānyamātra*) or the specific base (*prakṛta*). Therefore, since both possess meaning through the injunction of a qualified *bhāvanā*, there is an injunction of both; thus, it does not constitute a mere restatement (*anuvāda*). This being the case, being a name (*nāmatva*) is not the counter-correlative of being an injunction (*vidhitva*) alone; for those who [hold that] in the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) it is included within an injunction, but in the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) it serves the purpose of an injunction—

Their description of names as being something in excess of the ritual formulas (*vāda-mantra*) is indeed incorrect. Furthermore, because they constitute a factor for all worldly transactions (*vyavahāra*), they do not fail to produce specific activity. For instance, in the selection of priests (*ṛtvij-varaṇa*) and similar rites, the brief means of communication "I shall sacrifice with this" would not be possible [without names]. Likewise, when one is about to begin the *Darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices, the connection of an accessory (*guṇopabandha*) such as "One should perform the Darśapūrṇamāsa on level ground" [is only possible through names].

Furthermore, the connection with the fruit—expressed as "one desiring heaven [should sacrifice] by means of the Darśapūrṇamāsa"—would not be possible otherwise. Therefore, it is established that words of this kind are indeed names (nāmadheya). ||2||

There must be some basis for the application [of the suffix] to the object (*karman*). If the application to the object were made by adopting the sense of the *vat* suffix (the abstract suffix *-tva*), then that application would be extremely remote, resulting in a figurative usage (*gaugata*). In that case, it is better to resort to the indication of possession (*matvarthalakṣaṇā*). For when the means (*sādhana*) is understood, it conveys its own action to be accomplished (*sādhya*) without difficulty due to their absolute inseparability, even without the elision of the possessive suffix *-mat*. Furthermore—
The nominative case occurs when there is an intention to express the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*), excluding [the rule] beginning with "atha eṣa jyotiḥ.
However, that [intention] applies to the object (*karman*); for it is not the case that its application is determined by the case endings of the factors of action (*kāraka*).

But [the injunction] is by means of a rule (*vidhi*). Moreover, its essential nature (*svarūpa*) must also be made known. However, a quality (*guṇa*), whose form is already known, is to be employed as a factor of action (*kāraka*) through its case-endings; therefore, because there is no mention of the instrumental case (*tṛtīyā-nirdeśa*), if it is not an injunction of a quality, it is a name of the ritual action (*karmanāmadheya*). It is precisely relying on this position that the status of being the archetype (*prakṛtitva*) for the Jyotiṣṭoma was established in the *Udbhid-adhikaraṇa*.

For in the sentences concerning the hawk and so forth, no praise is seen on account of the understanding that "just as a hawk swoops down and seizes [its prey], so does this [sacrifice]," and by means of that [understanding], there must be a basis for what is being enjoined. [405] For a conventional designation established by a whole, when it has attained its own nature, necessarily subverts the conventional designation of its parts; for its acquisition of self-nature depends upon that [subversion].
